question.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Two Polynomials that Differ by a Constant Factor
question.problem: Find the least common multiple of $2(z-4)^{2}$ and $7(z-4)^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(2,7):$

- Multiples of $2:$ $\,2,\,4,…,\,12,\,14,16,…$

- Multiples of $7:$ $\,7,\,14,\,21,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(2,7)=14.$

Since the variable part is the same in the expressions, we have

$$
\text{LCM}((z-4)^{2},\,(z-4)^{2})=(z-4)^{2}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(2(z-4)^{2},\,7(z-4)^{2})=14\cdot (z-4)^{2}=14(z-4)^{2}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Two Single-Variable Polynomials
question.problem: Find the least common multiple of $10(y+1)^{6}$ and $15(y+1)^{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of two polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(10,15):$

- Multiples of $10:$ $\,10,\,20,\,30,\,40,…$

- Multiples of $15:$ $\,15,\,30,\,45,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(10,15)=30.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of $(y+1)^{6}$ and $(y+1)^{4},$ we raise $(y+1)$ to the largest power that appears in the expressions, which is $6.$ Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}((y+1)^{6},\,(y+1)^{4})=(y+1)^{6}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(10(y+1)^{6},\,15(y+1)^{4})=30\cdot (y+1)^{6}=30(y+1)^{6}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Three Polynomials
question.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $20{x}^{7}(y+2),$ $\,10{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},$ and $12{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of three polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(20,10,12):$

- Multiples of $20:$ $\,20,\,40,\,60,\,80,\,100,\,…$

- Multiples of $10:$ $\,10,\,20,\,30,\,40,\,50,\,60,\,70,\,…$

- Multiples of $12:$ $\,12,\,24,\,36,\,48,\,60,\,72,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(20,10,12)=60.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of ${x}^{7}(y+2),{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},$ and ${x}^{4}(y+2)^{2},$ we find the largest powers for $x$ and $(y+2)$ that appear in all these expressions:

- For ${x}^{7},\,{x}^{6},$ and ${x}^{4},$ the largest power is $7.$

- For $(y+2),(y+2)^{3},$ and $(y+2)^{2},$ the largest power is $3.$

Now, we raise $x$ and $(y+2)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}({x}^{7}(y+2),\,{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},\,{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2})={x}^{7}\cdot (y+2)^{3}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{LCM}(20{x}^{7}(y+2),\,10{x}^{6}(y+2)^{3},\,12{x}^{4}(y+2)^{2}) & = \\ 60\cdot {x}^{7}\cdot (y+2)^{3} & = \\ 60{x}^{7}(y+2)^{3} & .\end{aligned}
$$
